name: Xiao Chai Hu Tang (Xiaochaihu decoction; Japanese sho-saiko-to)
short: Pneumonitis with the Japanese version, sho-saiko-to (72 cases, 8 deaths; more with interferon-alpha). Liver injury: case reports and a hepatitis B record-data link. Little trial safety data.
text: Xiao Chai Hu Tang (Xiaochaihu decoction) is the same named formula as the Japanese Kampo medicine sho-saiko-to (also written syo-saiko-to or shosaikoto), and most reports of serious harm concern that Japanese preparation. A study in 26 healthy volunteers describes sho-saiko-to as a mixture of seven herbs: Bupleurum root, Pinellia tuber, Scutellaria root, jujube fruit, ginseng root, Glycyrrhiza (liquorice) root and ginger rhizome. Its most serious reported harm is lung inflammation (pneumonitis): of 94 cases reported to a drug maker in Japan, 72 were judged to be sho-saiko-to-induced pneumonitis, mostly in people taking it for hepatitis C-related liver disease, starting on average about 50 days into treatment; 64 survived after it was stopped or steroids were given, but 8 died of respiratory failure despite high-dose steroids. A Japanese report found pneumonitis in 0.7% of people with chronic hepatitis or cirrhosis given sho-saiko-to alone, 0.5% given interferon-alpha alone and 4.0% given both, and the authors conclude it is more likely when the two are given together. A review of 73 patients with pneumonitis from any Japanese herbal medicine found sho-saiko-to the most often used (26%); across all 73, 13 needed mechanical ventilation and 3 died. In the Japanese Adverse Drug Event Report database (2004 to 2018), sho-saiko-to had the third-highest of the ten reporting odds ratios the abstract gives for drug-induced interstitial lung disease (16.3, 95% CI 11.8 to 22.4), with a median time to onset of 33 days, and data mining suggested that the risk was increased by the combination of sho-saiko-to and older age; these are reports to the database, which show a reporting association, not how often it occurs. Case reports describe a 66-year-old woman with hepatitis C cirrhosis who died of respiratory failure and liver dysfunction after her interstitial pneumonitis relapsed (the authors suspect hepatitis C combined with sho-saiko-to lung injury), two women, aged 45 and 78, with non-cardiogenic fluid build-up in the lungs who needed mechanical ventilation and then improved (the 78-year-old was discharged), in both of whom a lymphocyte stimulation test was positive for shosaikoto, and acute eosinophilic pneumonia in a 16-year-old boy who had taken an over-the-counter cold remedy containing sho-saiko-to. A further case report describes a 7-year-old boy with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia and hepatitis C whose white-cell count fell when sho-saiko-to was given and who developed interstitial pneumonia when it was given again; his symptoms later improved. Liver injury is also reported: a 1995 report describes four patients with acute drug-induced liver injury after syo-saiko-to, starting one and a half to three months into treatment, in all of whom liver enzymes rose again after it was given again or in a challenge test (two had cholestasis); a 52-year-old woman developed acute hepatitis, confirmed on biopsy, after 1.5 months of the decoction and recovered after stopping it; a 67-year-old woman had liver injury after a 4-day course of drugs including shosaikoto extract, and again a year later with another formula that also contains Scutellariae radix; and in a Taiwanese insurance database study of people with hepatitis B (1,080 hospitalised liver-injury cases), herbal products containing radix bupleuri were associated with hospital admission for liver injury (adjusted odds ratio 1.90), with significantly high risk and a dose-response relationship for Xiao-Chai-Hu-Tang itself; this is an association in record data. A title-only record reports acute thrombocytopenic purpura (a low-platelet bleeding disorder) after sho-saiko-to taken for hepatitis. In the cited sources, evidence on low potassium is limited to a literature survey of 37 cases of licorice-induced pseudoaldosteronism, in which cases after sho-saiko-to developed after a median of 450 days (range 150 to 2,190); the abstract does not say how many of the 37 involved sho-saiko-to, and in the authors' own patients given sho-saiko-to, no negative correlation was observed between serum potassium and how long it had been taken; the pneumonitis review notes that such formulas commonly contain liquorice. On interactions, besides the interferon-alpha finding, the 26-volunteer study found that five days of sho-saiko-to lowered the activity of the drug-metabolising enzyme CYP1A2 (cytochrome P450 1A2) by 16% and of the enzyme xanthine oxidase by 20% to 25%, while CYP3A activity tended to be lower but not significantly (P = 0.146); these are enzyme measurements in healthy people, and the abstract does not name any affected medicine. In a 1989 double-blind multicentre trial in 222 people with chronic active hepatitis (116 given sho-saiko-to by mouth; the comparison group's placebo itself contained a small amount of the formula, and that group switched to the formula after 12 weeks), no remarkable side effects were noticed; the abstract gives no event counts. A 2019 Cochrane review of 10 randomized trials (934 participants) in chronic hepatitis B found that none aimed to assess serious adverse events, and the effect on non-serious adverse events was uncertain (very low-certainty evidence).
